zones.notes: Mandatory tread protection throughout all railing work. If riser spec was completed first, tread protection should already be in place — verify rather than re-install. Ram Board Stair Armor or equivalent non-slip protection. Standard plastic sheeting is EXTREME FALL HAZARD per Stairway_Systems_Doctrine Section 6.2.
Drop cloth runners at landing areas to protect finished floors.

zones.upgrade_scenario: Upgrades to heavy_mask when walls are SS_PAINTED_*
zones.notes: Wall masking for overspray containment when spraying balusters. Tape & Drape pre-taped plastic creates containment zones per doctrine 6.3. HVLP preferred over airless for in-place baluster work.

protection_zones_analysis.zone_reference: Protection_Zones_Reference.md v2.1 + stair_tread_covers zone (proposed in SF_STAIR_RISER_NC)
protection_zones_analysis.conditional_protection_note: Tread protection is UNCONDITIONAL. Floor protection conditional on floor_type. Wall masking conditional on spray method. Spray containment for balusters requires additional materials: cardboard shields, Tape & Drape, HVLP spray equipment.

adjacent_surfaces.notes: Baluster-to-handrail junction is the most labor-intensive edge in the railing system. In two-tone systems, relationship is different_finish — paint balusters first (light), handrail last (dark) to cover overlap at junction.
Balusters penetrate treads. Treads may be stain-grade or floor-rated coating. Not painted in this spec. Tread protection must be in place.
Handrail brackets attach through wall. At QT4+, brackets are removed and handrails finished horizontally. Wall-to-handrail edge occurs at bracket attachment points.
Newel base meets baseboard at landing level. Typically same color/sheen. Baseboard handled by SF_TRIM_NC_PAINT.
Risers are below balusters. If risers already painted (SF_STAIR_RISER_NC completed first), light masking needed at riser-to-baluster base junction.

adjacency_analysis.surface_reference: Surface_Vocabulary_Reference.md v1.0 — stair railing surfaces are NEW, not yet in vocabulary
adjacency_analysis.key_finding: Railing system painting is defined by JUNCTION COMPLEXITY, not surface area. The baluster-to-handrail junction is the dominant cost driver — taping 62 balusters takes ~2 hours vs. faster artist-brush cut-in technique. Two-tone systems amplify junction cost. Canonical painting sequence (balusters → newels → handrails) minimizes junction work in two-tone scenarios.

affected_conditions.notes: Landing floor protection required only when finished floors present.

affected_conditions.modifier_notes: occupied_sensitive triggers OCC_SENSITIVE modifier 1.30x on protection tasks per Modifier_Registry
affected_conditions.notes: Additional protection when occupied. Rare in NC context.

affected_conditions.modifier_notes: tested_positive triggers LEAD_POSITIVE modifier 2.00x per Modifier_Registry. Rare in NC.
affected_conditions.notes: Railings, balusters, and newels are among the components most likely to carry lead paint in pre-1978 homes per doctrine 13.2. Extremely rare in NC context.

input_states.description: Uncoated wood or bare iron railing components requiring full primer
input_states.notes: Wood: standard millwork primer per substrate. Iron: DTM acrylic primer (SSPC-SP 1 solvent cleaning mandatory before any primer).

input_states.description: Factory-primed wood components — skip primer, lighter prep
input_states.notes: Standard NC — wood components arrive pre-primed from mill. Scuff sand for adhesion.

input_states.description: Iron balusters with factory powder coat — bonding primer required after scuff-sand
input_states.notes: Applies to iron balusters when railing_type=iron_and_wood. Scuff-sand with 180-220 grit. Bonding primer only — self-etching primers do NOT work on powder coat per doctrine 4.4.

relevant_findings.finding: Balusters have the highest per-unit labor density of any stairway component. Square balusters: 3-5 min/EA per coat. Turned/ornate: 5-10 min/EA per coat. A system with 62 balusters at 3 coats = 930-1860 minutes of baluster painting alone.
relevant_findings.impact: Baluster count is the primary cost driver. Production rate varies 2x between square and turned profiles.

relevant_findings.finding: One painter works each side of the baluster simultaneously, dramatically increasing throughput on large baluster counts.
relevant_findings.impact: Conditional technique for large baluster counts. Not modeled as separate task — captured in production rate variability.

relevant_findings.topic: Artist brush vs taping at junctions
relevant_findings.finding: Taping 62 balusters at the baluster-rail junction takes ~2 hours. Artist brush cut-in is faster and produces cleaner results. German round trim brushes (1.25 inch) are purpose-made for turned baluster profiles.
relevant_findings.impact: Technique selection affects time but not task structure. Both approaches accomplish the same task.

relevant_findings.finding: On two-tone systems, coat the entire handrail underside in the baluster color to eliminate precise cutting-in at the junction — the underside is rarely inspected.
relevant_findings.impact: Reduces junction labor in two-tone scenarios. Finish group decision, not spec-level config.

relevant_findings.finding: Per SSPC-SP 1, ALL iron/steel balusters must receive solvent cleaning before any primer. Oils and drawing compounds from manufacturing cause fish-eye defects and delamination.
relevant_findings.impact: Mandatory prep step for iron balusters. Non-negotiable regardless of quality tier.

relevant_findings.finding: Remove handrails and brackets, label and bag each piece, paint behind attachment points, finish handrails horizontally to reduce runs/sags, then reinstall.
relevant_findings.impact: QT4+ technique. Requires dedicated prep and reinstall tasks. At QT3, brackets are masked in place.

relevant_findings.finding: HVLP sprayers produce significantly less overspray than airless and are preferred for in-place baluster work. When using airless: fine-finish tips (Graco FFLP 108, 210/310 series, 4-6 inch fan).
relevant_findings.impact: Spray method selection affects containment requirements and material waste.

relevant_findings.finding: Some professionals apply a polyurethane topcoat over paint on handrails for additional hand-oil resistance.
relevant_findings.impact: Optional QT5 upgrade. Additional clear coat on handrails only.

relevant_findings.finding: Adding extender (Floetrol for latex, Penetrol for alkyd) improves leveling and extends working time on detail-intensive baluster work. Prevents roping on complex profiles.
relevant_findings.impact: Material recommendation for brush application on turned balusters.

square vs turned drives production rate (2x difference)
QT3=spot sand, QT4=full sand + bracket removal, QT5=thorough sand + feel test + optional poly
brush vs spray drives containment requirements and production rates
High count (62+) may justify spray + two-person technique

failure_modes.cause: Spray tip too far, insufficient material flow
failure_modes.prevention: 6-8 inch distance, fine-finish tips, bottom-to-top for primer

failure_modes.prevention: Flow additive (Floetrol/Penetrol), German round trim brushes

Using self-etching primer instead of bonding primer

Add SYS_PRIMER_IRON_DTM for bare iron balusters — new substrate-driven primer
Add SYS_PRIMER_POWDER_COAT_BOND for powder-coated iron — bonding primer after scuff-sand
Reuse SYS_PRIMER_* wood primer systems from riser spec where applicable

New consumable: CON_SCOTCH_BRITE_PAD for iron baluster scuff-sand

Reuse CON_STAIR_ARMOR, CON_MASKING_TAPE_SAFE_RELEASE from riser spec

notes_for_sop_librarian: Iron baluster solvent cleaning is FIRST prep step (before any sanding)
Handrail bracket removal at QT4+ — separate prep/reinstall tasks
Spray containment setup is a protection task (spray method only)
Tread protection VERIFY task (not install — may already be in place from riser spec)
Optional poly topcoat task on handrails at QT5
Feel test on handrails at QT5 final inspection
Base rail tasks are CONDITIONAL on system having base rail
notes_for_estimation_engineer: Baluster rates from doctrine Section 9.2: square 3-5 min/EA, turned 5-10 min/EA per coat
Use 4 min/EA for square (midpoint), 7 min/EA for turned (midpoint) as baseline brush rates
Newel rates: ~10-15 min/EA per coat (larger, more detail than balusters)
Handrail rates: comparable to trim LF rates but slower due to 4-surface coverage (top, 2 sides, underside)
H1 for all components — no height modifier
baluster_profile modifier: square=1.0, turned=1.75 (ratio of 7/4 midpoint times)
Spray rates: 2-3x faster than brush for balusters but containment setup offsets some of the gain
No access staging overhead modeled per-task — project-level factor
Taping approach: ~2 min/EA for baluster junction taping (incorporated into brush finish rate)

assumptions.assumption: Baluster production rates from Stairway_Systems_Doctrine Section 9.2 are per-coat brush rates
Newel post production rates derived from baluster rates scaled by relative size (2-3x larger)
Handrail rates comparable to trim LF but 25% slower due to 4-surface access
Base rail rates same as handrail rates (similar LF-based linear surface)
Iron baluster solvent cleaning adds ~1 min/EA to prep
